title: Fermionic pairs, from the surface to the bulk
authors: Sandra Brandstetter, Carl Heintze, Fabian Brauneis, Stephanie M. Reimann, Georg Bruun, Maciej Gałka, Selim Jochim
abstract: Fermion pairing underlies collective quantum phenomena across widely different forms of matter. In extended systems such as ultracold Fermi gases, pairing is commonly understood through the BCS--BEC crossover, where the pair size evolves from large, overlapping Cooper pairs to tightly bound dimers. In finite systems such as atomic nuclei, superconducting grains and quantum dots, however, the same pairing tendency competes with confinement, shell filling and spatial inhomogeneity, making the microscopic structure of pairs much harder to access. Here, we image pair correlations in a finite, tunable system of few fermionic atoms with single-particle resolution and full counting statistics. We observe that confinement and shell structure re-organize pairing in real space: In the weakly interacting, confinement-dominated regime, closed-shell configurations suppress correlations in the high-density trap center. Pairing is mainly observed toward the low-density surface. Open-shell systems, however, support substantially stronger central pairing. Already for surprisingly small systems, increasing either interaction strength or particle number restores a locally bulk-like Cooper-pair profile in the trap center, whereas the edge retains dimer-like correlations. By resolving where pairs form and how their character changes from localized dimers to overlapping Cooper pairs, our measurements provide a microscopic view of pairing in finite fermionic matter and connect the physics of mesoscopic cold atoms to pairing phenomena in nuclei and superconducting nanostructures.
summary: This work experimentally images fermionic pair correlations in few-atom trapped systems to understand pairing beyond the standard BCS-BEC crossover. By analyzing real-space correlations, the authors show that confinement and shell effects dictate where pairs form, revealing distinct surface versus bulk behaviors depending on whether the atomic shell is open or closed.
main_problem: The study investigates fermionic pairing correlations in finite, trapped systems, contrasting with the well-understood BCS–BEC crossover seen in extended media.
main_result: Pairing structure is highly sensitive to confinement and shell filling; closed shells suppress central pairing, while open shells support stronger central pairing, showing a transition from dimer-like edge correlations to bulk Cooper pairs centrally.
method: The work combines single-atom resolution imaging of pair correlation functions ($C^{(2)}$) with theoretical modeling using BCS mean-field theory and exact diagonalization for few-body limits.
model_or_system: The system uses ultracold fermionic atoms (e.g., ${}^6	ext{Li}$) confined in a quasi-2D trap, allowing control over interaction strength ($E_B$) relative to confinement scales ($\ell, r_F$).
key_observables: Real and momentum space pair correlation functions ($C^{(2)}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r})$ and $C^{(2)}(\mathbf{p}, -\mathbf{p})$), and the pairing gap $\Delta$.
important_parameters: The relative sizes of three length scales: mean interparticle spacing ($\ell$), pair size ($r_B$), and system size ($r_F$); open vs. closed shell configurations.
main_assumptions: Theoretical analysis relies on BCS theory, Local Density Approximation (LDA), and the assumption that finite resolution effects regularize divergences in correlation functions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the three pairing regimes based on length scale ratios; measured pair correlations are shown for varying interactions, comparing open vs. closed shell behavior across different system sizes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the problem (finite vs. bulk pairing) to detailing measurements of correlation functions in various regimes (molecular, intermediate, confinement-dominated), culminating in a comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental observations for open/closed shells.
why_interesting: It provides crucial microscopic insights into how boundary conditions and quantum shell structure modify fundamental many-body phenomena like superconductivity, bridging cold atom physics to nuclear structure models.
